readerTitle: Same facts, different words: why the frame decides
caseNote: 가상 사례 (바닷가 호텔, 급여 대행 회사, IT 지원 회사) + 실제 연구 (Levin & Gaeth, 1988 다진 소고기 라벨 실험)
insight: 사실을 설명하는 중립적인 방법은 없다. 모든 문장은 이미 하나의 프레임을 고른 것이므로, 프레임은 우연에 맡기지 말고 의도적으로 고른다.
misconception: 사실만 정확하면 어떻게 표현하든 고객의 판단은 같다.

sources.text: Levin, I. P., & Gaeth, G. J. (1988). How consumers are affected by the framing of attribute information before and after consuming the product. Journal of Consumer Research, 15(3), 374–378.
호텔, 급여 대행, IT 지원 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Levin & Gaeth(1988): '75% lean' 라벨 집단이 '25% fat' 집단보다 품질을 높게, 기름기를 적게 평가했고, 시식 후에는 차이가 줄었지만 남아 있었다는 내용을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two businesses, two true facts, and the words did the work.
body: A seaside hotel has a cancellation rule. A payroll firm has a one-year track record. Both facts are true, and both can be said in a way that sounds good or a way that sounds worrying.
Neither business changes what it does. It only changes how it says it. Customers' choices change anyway.

image.label: Two shop signs with the same fact in different words
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 작은 바닷가 호텔 프런트, 오른쪽에 사무실 책상. 두 곳 모두 말풍선 두 개가 떠 있고, 하나는 따뜻한 색, 하나는 차가운 색. 글자는 넣지 않거나 흐리게. 실제 로고·상표 없음.

cards.title: One line for your booking page.
body: You run a 20-room seaside hotel. Guests can cancel for free until 48 hours before arrival. After that, they pay for the first night.
Your booking page has room for one line about the policy. Which do you choose?

options.text: "Cancellations within 48 hours of arrival are charged one night."
options.feedback: Clear and honest, and it heads off disputes. But it leads with the penalty, so a guest who is still deciding sees the risk first.
Same rule, but the guest first sees what they keep: freedom to change plans. Put the one-night charge right below it so nobody is surprised later.

options.text: Either one. The rule is the same, so the wording won't matter.
options.feedback: The rule is the same, but people react to what you put in front of them. Treating wording as neutral just means it gets chosen by accident.

cards.title: One fact each, two honest ways to say it.
body: Across town, a payroll firm ran 200 payrolls for small businesses last year. One was late. Like the hotel, it has two true versions to choose from. Neither is a lie, but each leaves a different feeling.

breakdown.label: Payroll · success side
breakdown.detail: Of payrolls ran on time last year

breakdown.label: Payroll · failure side
breakdown.detail: Payroll runs were late last year

cards.title: Framing
body: **Framing** is how you present a fact: which side you put first, which number you use, and what you compare it to. The facts stay the same. The choices people make often don't.
Here's the new way to see it: there is no neutral way to say something. Every sentence already picks a frame. The only question is whether you picked it on purpose.

image.label: One fact passing through two different picture frames
image.brief: 가운데 같은 모양의 상자 하나(사실)가 있고, 왼쪽에는 밝은 액자, 오른쪽에는 어두운 액자를 통해 보이는 장면. 액자에 따라 상자를 보는 사람의 표정이 다름. 텍스트 최소화.

cards.title: 75% lean or 25% fat?
body: In a 1988 study, researchers Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth asked people to rate ground beef. Some saw it labeled **75% lean**. Others saw **25% fat**. It was the same beef.
People who saw "75% lean" rated it as higher quality and less greasy. After they actually tasted it, the gap got smaller, but it did not disappear.
The label changed how the same product seemed, even in the mouth.

cards.title: Frames come in more than one shape.
body: Choosing the bright side or the dark side is only one kind of frame. You also choose the unit and the comparison.
list: **Gain or loss:** "save $200 a month" or "stop losing $200 a month"
**Unit:** per year, per month, per person or per use
**Comparison:** next to what? A $40 lunch feels different next to a $15 one than next to a $90 dinner
cards.callout: The best frame usually matches how the customer already thinks about the decision.
cards.softwareNote: A software company can say "99.9% uptime" or "down about 9 hours a year". Both are true. A buyer planning around outages may care more about the second.

cards.title: A frame can clarify or it can hide.
body: If the hotel buried the one-night charge, it might win the booking and lose the review. A frame that hides the bad part borrows trust it will have to repay.

Frames also weaken with experience, as the beef tasters showed. And careful buyers, like a finance team, often convert every frame back to the same number. With them, a clear and honest frame earns more than a clever one.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You sell managed IT support to a 12-person accounting office for $600 a month. The office manager has to get the owner to approve it.
How do you put the price in your proposal?

options.feedback: Honest and easy to budget if the owner plans yearly. But one big number with no comparison makes the cost feel heavy and the value invisible.

options.text: "$50 per employee per month, less than the cost of one lost day when systems go down"
options.feedback: It uses a unit the owner already thinks in, cost per person, and compares it to the risk it removes. The comparison has to be realistic for this office, or it backfires.
The number is small, but business buyers know the trick and multiply it back. It can make a serious service sound like a late-night ad.

cards.title: You always choose a frame, so choose it on purpose.
body: Same facts, different words, different decisions. Pick the side, the unit and the comparison that match how your customer decides, and never hide the part they need to know.
**Try it today:** take one line from your price list or website. Write it two other honest ways. Ask a customer which one is clearest.
